letterboxd-review-1537730190.title: Heat
letterboxd-review-1537730190.review:
What are you doing?

What am I doing? I'm talking to an empty telephone.

I don't understand.

'Cause there is a dead man on the other end of this fucking line.

letterboxd-review-1536442211.title: Ink
letterboxd-review-1536442211.review: a legacy steeped in sensationalism. solidly entertaining throughout as a fast, high-tension telling of the birth and damage of one of the worst populist publications to ever exist. Very funny early on, with lots of tricky visual elements, but Boyle's eccentricities don't meet the moral core of it all that well in its final act. And it concludes with the most horribly meaningless gen-ai image, obviously dampens what is otherwise a pretty good watch. conflicted. Boyle was the chosen one.

letterboxd-review-1535471949.title: Misty Green
letterboxd-review-1535471949.review: for the most part, it's nonsense; the shallowest sprint - emphasis on sprint - through hollywood’s underworld. something we’ve repeatedly seen. But occasionally, for some bizarre reason, it's oddly entertaining - like awful television you can't stop watching. Rosalind Eleazar is very good. Also great to see Kaluuya on the big screen again.

letterboxd-review-1535021650.title: Congo Boy
letterboxd-review-1535021650.review: in this life, we cannot hide.

letterboxd-review-1534112346.title: Primetime
letterboxd-review-1534112346.review:
the morbid voyeristic nature inherent to reality tv, documentaries transformed into artifice in order to lure the next big crowd. Performance at the core. Prior to the showing, Lance Oppenheim highlighted Kiarostami‘a
Close-Up
as the main inspiration behind this, which makes all the sense in the world. Pattinson is scary great, but Weaver and Gisondo are just as good. So many cool formal experiments here.

letterboxd-review-1533263919.title: Wildwood
letterboxd-review-1533263919.review: I can't stress enough how ridiculous it is that we're still getting creations like this, and how crucial it is that we help keep them alive. essentially a ginormous structural homage to many of the great high-fantasy works - there's a Pelennor Fields-style charge that completely overwhelmed me. a life-affirming wonder. Loved it.

letterboxd-review-1532180290.title: Paper Tiger
letterboxd-review-1532180290.review: plays as a gloomy macho crime drama pretty steadily until it completely engulfs you in its god-like final act - the tall grass sequence is mythical filmmaking. The breakdown of an American dream layered in Greek tragedy.

letterboxd-review-1531580893.title: Ray Gunn
letterboxd-review-1531580893.review: a silly neo-noir/sci-fi mashup that Brad Bird has obviously been working towards his entire career. brimming with so many reflections on the grimness of our world today - ai, the sharp decline in personal autonomy, the unchecked power of corporate elites. heart on sleeve type stuff, and although occasionally muddled with its parables, it’s a great time. Thoroughly enjoyed.

letterboxd-review-1531192105.title: Wild Horse Nine
letterboxd-review-1531192105.review:
It's really really similar to
In Bruges
- not quite as good, but the conclusion is so rewarding. Incredibly sombre, a thorough reckoning with mortality that plays with the line between political conspiracy and personal tragedy. John Malkovich is fantastic. It does lack the bite of McDonagh's best stuff; I simply don't think his work with American actors is as effective in a darkly comedic way. Also has a brilliant image reference to Ford’s
The Searchers
so points for that.

letterboxd-review-1530524313.title: The Devils
letterboxd-review-1530524313.review: ascended through the roof on numerous occasions - how does this even exist? fucking hell. Has some of the best staging I’ve ever seen, the production has to be seen to be believed. Descends into the darkest depths of religious fanaticism, a nasty nightmare in every sense. Switches from silly to bloodcurdling so seamlessly. Kermode’s intro was the greatest I’ve ever sat through.

letterboxd-review-1530062043.title: Elsinore
letterboxd-review-1530062043.review:
liked the ideas it plays with in terms of the pursuit of an artistic high, even during the darkest days. Equipped with a couple life-affirming showreels thrown in. Andrew Scott is excellent (of course), but the direction is so cold and still: rarely allows for any reflection and is formally a little dull. Probably the most by the book, against-the-odds story that your grandma will probably love. Hits you over the head with everything it wants to tell you. the
Hamnet
for me of this year, waiting for that emotional explosion but it never arrived.

letterboxd-review-1529938919.title: The Man I Love
letterboxd-review-1529938919.review:
Brimming with so many incredible portraits: strikes some of the most delicate images of the year. Self-expression until the very end - such a brilliant artistic tribute. Rami Malek is revelatory.
It’s a tough business, living
.

letterboxd-review-1529300555.title: La Bola Negra
letterboxd-review-1529300555.review: Extremely well-staged. So much texture to it, the environments feel so lived-in and tangible, each era is so visually distinct. Revels in its spectacle. That being said, man the period switches took me right out of the central tragedy at times: constant shifts from being right there ready to be unbelievably moved to a loss of impetus - a constant reach for a moment that never truly arrived. Not a risk in sight narratively. Need to sit with this a little.

letterboxd-review-1529005126.title: The Beloved
letterboxd-review-1529005126.review: Formally impressive, operating with some visual ideas that actually aid rather than come across as gimmicky obstacles. Thought I was going to hate it during the first 30 minutes: the coldness from the central relationship really seeped into the idea. I was getting virtually nothing from it. But, there’s a particular scene about an hour in where the meta-statement finally starts to hit. The final act is good stuff. Really liked the black & white bits, great lingering moments of angst.

letterboxd-review-1527757822.title: Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Man's Chest
letterboxd-review-1527757822.review: so glad they only made three of these things: as soon as they realised Gore Verbinski wouldn't be back for the fourth to add his wonderfully gritty sensibilities once again, they scrapped it. Perfect call if you ask me. What a trilogy.

letterboxd-review-1524186294.title: Crooklyn
letterboxd-review-1524186294.review: Then it's good she died … so she wouldn't have to suffer.

letterboxd-review-1521660756.title: Digger
letterboxd-review-1521660756.review: indulges in its little meta gimmick too much, never completely committing to its own self-proclaimed powerful concept. But, at the end of the day, art will aways bring people together, even on the darkest of days - and it posits this well. Comes together nicely (after a very poor start), with a standout final moment that feels like a glimpse into a future not beyond the realms of possibility. Plemons is the man. I imagine this one will be ready for reclamation in 5 years or so.

letterboxd-review-1519857991.title: The Adventures of Sharkboy and Lavagirl
letterboxd-review-1519857991.review: Dream, dream, dream, dream, dream, dream.

letterboxd-review-1518828652.title: Hope
letterboxd-review-1518828652.review:
Overly long galaxy-brained nonsense really.
Bay
-esque in lots of ways, and when it’s at its best, it’s absolutely blistering. It took me a second to lose myself in the universe as it deviated between the spills and thrills, but it wasn’t too long until I was fully locked in. Shockingly bizarre (complimentary), and the final chase made me feel as if I’d been injected with pure rocket fuel. Loses steam far too much to be an action great of this era, but its sheer lunacy can only be respected.

letterboxd-review-1516064902.title: The Immigrant
letterboxd-review-1516064902.review: The half-mirror, half-window final frame could not work any better. Both heading off into uncertain futures in an exhausted America. A bittersweet moment of survival for Ewa. Marion Cotillard is unbelievable here.

letterboxd-review-1510382654.title: Her Private Hell
letterboxd-review-1510382654.review:
I found it a little cold at times, similar to
The Neon Demon
, but Refn has such a talent at creating these dream-like, nightmarish worlds brimming with a glossy artifice. A misty city covered in fog, bending time in countless ways, being both past and present. Refn going full Refn. A walking dream. Probably my favourite of his since
Drive
- does almost feel like the child of the 2 that came before it.

letterboxd-review-1508954805.title: The Texas Chain Saw Massacre
letterboxd-review-1508954805.review: The purest horror film to ever exist. I want to replay RE7: Biohazard now.

letterboxd-review-1507455037.title: Babel
letterboxd-review-1507455037.review:
a really cheap, misery-filled multilayered tale in which tragedies are carelessly pushed together in order to make a heavy-handed statement about connectivity. And, unlike
Amores Perros
(which I mostly really liked), its persistent sorrow hinders rather than helps. Not the worst thing in the world, but this is definitely the first of Inarritu’s films that I’ve outright disliked.

letterboxd-review-1506726037.title: Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker's Apocalypse
letterboxd-review-1506726037.review: my greatest fear is to make a really shitty, embarrassing, pompous film on an important subject, and i am doing it. and i confront it. i acknowledge, i will tell you right straight from... the most sincere depths of my heart, the film will not be good.

letterboxd-review-1506547691.title: The Mandalorian and Grogu
letterboxd-review-1506547691.review:
Pretty harmless, not quite
TROS
bad, but still quite bad. It has virtually no visual identity at all and consists of flat frame after flat frame with little to no care behind them. It's made worse by the fact that there's just nothing here really on an emotional level: at least with
TROS
, I was actively annoyed whilst watching. Take a risk! Bring the emotion back!

letterboxd-review-1502501900.title: eXistenZ
letterboxd-review-1502501900.review: Snaps back and forth between virtual and actual, one reality within another, human existence moulded by social systems. Defies expectations from every angle. So weird and stilted in every way (proper old-school video game stuff), and for my money, Cronenberg's best effort.

letterboxd-review-1498633246.title: Resident Evil
letterboxd-review-1498633246.review: Silly one-liners, exaggerated slimy monstrosities, and a strong emphasis on unskilled vulnerability. Something that switches from terrified POV images as our guy cautiously enters a room or turns a corner to deafeningly loud intrusions of complete freaks in a blink. Like the games, there are a ton of ridiculous obstacles in this - I have also tried to shoot off my fair share of locks as Ethan Winters. Austin Abrams nails it as the perfect everyman, he is remarkably funny. Plays out with many of the strongest elements from the games: the anxiousness of re2, the survival roots of re7, and one-liners similar to those Leon would say in re4. I can't even begin to express how hilarious I thought it was, even when the ideas are subtly undermined by its own absurdity. One of the funniest things I’ve seen in years.

letterboxd-review-1496166280.title: The Fire Within: A Requiem for Katia and Maurice Krafft
letterboxd-review-1496166280.review: The untamed, formidable power of nature. An awe-inspiring eulogy - Herzog is one of the greatest minds of our time. Without question.

letterboxd-review-1496039534.title: Pather Panchali
letterboxd-review-1496039534.review: Uses the most authentic techniques to capture genuine humanity in the day-to-day hardships of poverty. The environments are shot with such grace: full of dense trees, flowers, and narrow pathways. Man, that train scene - the perfect urban contrast to their static, rural lives. Has such a way of showing childlike wonder even during its worst moments. Looking forward to continuing the trilogy!

letterboxd-review-1493148128.title: The Matrix
letterboxd-review-1493148128.review:
career-best work from virtually everyone involved. The lobby shootout shakes me to my very core. No major Hollywood release has had fights scenes as good since - Yuen Woo-ping is the man. Actually a medium-altering creation: there is cinema pre-
matrix
and post-
matrix
. As good as it gets.

letterboxd-review-1491571180.title: The Son
letterboxd-review-1491571180.review:
Hard to believe that this came from the same guy who wrote and directed
The Father.
Honestly, this is pretty disgraceful, and so reliant on its overly-dramatised, hackneyed moments. Let’s hope
The Bunker
is better - much better!

letterboxd-review-1489587323.title: The Handmaiden
letterboxd-review-1489587323.review: So unbelievably calculated at every step. Literally a painting in motion - frame after frame of the most outrageously well-constructed compositions. A complex structure that never loses sight of its central idea: liberation. First watch in years, and it was a needed one. Park Chan Wook is truly a wizard. Insane stuff.

letterboxd-review-1488144324.title: On the Waterfront
letterboxd-review-1488144324.review: Very significant blindspot checked off for the current performance list I'm doing. Really appreciate how simplistic it is, with the hyper-realistic setting emphasising the true misery of the day-to-day for the dockworkers: lots of shivering, mist and busy confined streets. Didn’t completely love it, but it does a great job of immersing you as though you’re actually there. Brando is pretty good, I guess.

letterboxd-review-1488083728.title: A Woman Under the Influence
letterboxd-review-1488083728.review: Full to the brim with devastating spirals and emotional changes, portrayed in such close-up, merciless detail. every shot accentuates Gena Rowland's flawless representation of fragility, moments that shift from quiet to frantic in an instant. In many ways, Rowland is too fucking good: it's scary how real everything feels, especially in the second half. Sat waiting for her impending destruction as she tries to live up to the ideal while suppressing her own nature, trapped in a loop. The scene where the doctor visits is absolutely horrible. Truly heartbreaking and as good as so many have stated. Actually watched this a couple of days ago, but wanted to sit with it a little longer (very rare for me). and yes, this finally means I’ll be going through one of my darkest blind spots: Cassavetes‘ filmography. Safe to say my expectations are very high now.

letterboxd-review-1484171347.title: Possession
letterboxd-review-1484171347.review: Isabelle Adjani's visceral descent in this is simply breathtaking: truly in the pantheon of horror performances. Full-tilt in the best conceivable way. The tight close-ups made it feel like she was staring directly into my soul.

letterboxd-review-1481804695.title: Mad Max: Fury Road
letterboxd-review-1481804695.review:
Plays so perfectly off the back of
Furiosa
, amplifying the grotesque rage and the metallic rhythms. Every scarred Furiosa look bears the mark of over a decade of complete tyranny. Mythical filmmaking. Absolutely fucking insane.

letterboxd-review-1480649335.title: Deadpool 2
letterboxd-review-1480649335.review: I still mostly loathe Deadpool's obnoxious meta-schtick, but it feels a little more restrained here. I can't believe how serviceable this one is compared to the first: Its crude moments of violence actually compliment the sad undercurrent, and they do so with a smidge of style! Nothing special at all, but Leitch's effort is at least bold in ways. I was very much expecting to hate this.

letterboxd-review-1478049519.title: Taste of Cherry
letterboxd-review-1478049519.review: You can sympathize, understand, show compassion. But feel my pain? No. You suffer and so do I. I understand you. You comprehend my pain, but you can't feel it

letterboxd-review-1475408190.title: Close-Up
letterboxd-review-1475408190.review: Always love films about films: they scratch a special itch, and this is that in its most bizarre and meta form. Carries this really unique emotional nature, so conscious of what makes the form so special and transformative. Really great.

letterboxd-review-1474876016.title: Batman: Knightfall Part 1: Knightfall
letterboxd-review-1474876016.review: Seriously menacing stuff, establishes its darkness early on and gradually intensifies the psychological toll on Batman as it progresses. The transformation into the crazy battle-figure-type Bane is so cool and the subsequent assault bit is truly wicked. It's a little rough around the edges and rushed (bit overwhelming at times), but this is some really really solid stuff. Truly embraces the gloom of Gotham.

letterboxd-review-1471943626.title: Superbad
letterboxd-review-1471943626.review: One of the funniest things ever made: full of truly generational quips and the silliest back-and-forths around each corner. It perfectly captures those youthful anxieties - the type of state you'd fall into when attempting to fit in, the awkwardness that would grab you and refuse to let go. This is the ultimate day-in-the-life play, 24 hours of chaos. So seminal for me not only because of how much I remember crying with laughter when I first got it on DVD back in the late 2000s, but mostly because of its formidable relatability during my late-teens - learning to let go of times gone by. Michael Cera gives one of the greatest comedic performances of all time.

letterboxd-review-1471704716.title: Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look
letterboxd-review-1471704716.review: consider this review my official formal apology to everyone I have a real-life relationship with: you may never see me again from the 19th of November. Not a blade of grass shall be touched.

letterboxd-review-1470332413.title: 6 Underground
letterboxd-review-1470332413.review: It has to be said: this is complete nonsense. Truly one of the most ridiculous things I've ever seen. Bay at his most insane and maximalist, an unchecked projection of his hyper-masculine sensibilities. Even a little much for me at times, but it does carry this energy that is so uniquely him. I actually had an alright time with this (mostly).

letterboxd-review-1469033050.title: The Devil Wears Prada
letterboxd-review-1469033050.review: I love Meryl Streep's entrance in this: the epitome of cinematic evil. Vader-type stuff. Had her imperial officers trembling at the mere thought of her.

letterboxd-review-1468951174.title: Sanshiro Sugata
letterboxd-review-1468951174.review: It's an odd one to even criticise given how much of it was torn apart post-release, and you can tell since it feels fragmented. But despite the fact that this was his first feature, Kurosawa's visual flair is still so present, particularly in the way the environments are handled and how it’s so tightly framed.

letterboxd-review-1467503362.title: Caché
letterboxd-review-1467503362.review:
up there as one of the most thematically-dense creations ever. structured around its smallest
moments, where each and every watch will have you noticing something new. Always something
hidden
in plain sight.

letterboxd-review-1459820427.title: Leviticus
letterboxd-review-1459820427.review: Really wanted to love this, but as the credits began to roll, I simply didn’t feel much at all. I adore the sentiment at work and appreciate how confrontational it is. It so often felt like it was getting somewhere with its characters and reaching this special point of vulnerability, only to be derailed by a number of pretty poor horror elements. Obviously bursting with ideas, but perhaps wears its influences too overtly.

letterboxd-review-1459707736.title: Our Hero, Balthazar
letterboxd-review-1459707736.review: There is very clearly something to be said about gen Z’s  fascination with tragedy, especially within an era where every little detail is so readily accessible. This reckons with that obsession along with how damaging isolation can be in conjunction. I was quite struck by how raw and honest this is. Never really know what’s to come next from both of the duo - it constantly shows how they have been shaped by the messed up world they live in. Two opposing struggles with loneliness. Asa Butterfield is very good. Not perfect, and a little heavy-handed, but a really really solid debut.

letterboxd-review-1546615707.title: Faces of Death
letterboxd-review-1546615707.review: taps in so well to online fears and the ongoing exposure to violence. the commodification of exploitative content, viewed as just that — content. wickedly critiques the never-ending cycle of the priority for so many that is engagement. complicity from behind the screen. maybe shoots for more of an ambitious nature than it can handle at times, but as a pointed confrontation at today’s digitally-driven landscape, I think it’s a massive success. Sure, it’s on-the-nose stuff, but I actually really liked it.

letterboxd-review-1545284998.title: Nocturnal Animals
letterboxd-review-1545284998.review: a jarring provocation that’s unsure whether it’s coming or going: feels almost insidious in many ways. simply the most hollow meta-framework. There’s some pretty cool and distinct visual styles at play here and but as you look past them, you realise how fundamentally stupid it all is. the unevenness does contribute to how strangely fascinating it can be at times, though! almost want to stop watching but can’t type-stuff.

letterboxd-review-1545259264.title: Encounters at the End of the World
letterboxd-review-1545259264.review:
My grandmother was reading the Odyssey and the Iliad to me. So I started my journey in my fantasy before I even knew the means of accomplishing it, but my mind and my psyche was ready for it. I was already travelling with Odysseus and with the Argonauts and to those strange and amazing lands. That always stayed with me, that fascination of the world, and I fell in love with the world.

Searching for meaning at the end of the earth. Professional dreamers.

letterboxd-review-1549354230.title: The Texas Chainsaw Massacre
letterboxd-review-1549354230.review:
Satisfyingly grim like the original in many ways: full of decay, copious amounts of sweat, and environments that are horrible enough to elicit physical reactions on their own
- House of Wax
remake-like. It replaces the original's hints of violence with more obvious bursts of savagery, which is essentially why it fails to work as effectively. It takes away a lot of the thought, but it's still a good good remake. Do not care much for the hitchhiker scene in this one, though. Imagine if Zombie directed this one instead.
